title: Landforms and Erosion
seo_title: Grade 3 Science: Landforms and Erosion Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Wind, water and ice change the shape of the land: major local landforms (mountains, valleys, deltas, glaciers), First Peoples knowledge of local landforms, and changes caused by erosion and deposition. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Science 3, Earth and Space Science)
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 science worksheets (BC): weathering, erosion and deposition by wind, water and ice, fast and slow changes, and protecting land. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Wind, water and ice wear down and move the land.
key_sub: Weathering breaks rock; erosion carries it away.
body_html:
How to think about it

Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces (ice in cracks, plant roots, rain). Erosion moves the pieces away with water, wind or glaciers, and deposition drops them somewhere else. Rivers carve valleys and build deltas where they meet the sea, like the Fraser River delta.

Most changes are slow and take thousands of years, but floods, landslides and storms can change the land in hours. Plant roots help hold soil in place.

Example

Sand piles up where a river meets the ocean. What is this called?

The river drops what it carried.

Answer: deposition (a delta)

Example

What carved the U-shaped valleys in BC's mountains?

Huge sheets of moving ice

Answer: glaciers

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up weathering (breaking) and erosion (moving).
  • Thinking all landforms change quickly.
  • Forgetting that ice is an agent of erosion.

faq.a: Plant grass and trees, build walls, and keep soil covered.
Waves carry sand away in storms and drop it back in calm weather.

items.q: Sofia finds an old photo of a big rock and a new photo of the same rock, only a bit smaller after 100 years. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It took 100 years to change a little.

items.q: In the desert, rock heats up by day and cools at night until thin layers flake off. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: Which of these is caused by deposition?
c: a sandbar at the mouth of a creek
a cliff falling into the sea
items.e: A sandbar forms where sand is dropped.

items.q: Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone and makes a cave. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: A glacier carries boulders as it slowly moves down a valley. Which process is this?
items.e: Transportation carries the pieces to a new place.

items.q: Ocean waves crash against a rocky shore. What happens to the rocks over time?
c: They are broken and smoothed into pebbles and sand.
items.e: Waves are an agent of erosion.

items.q: A river slows down where it meets the sea and drops mud, forming new land. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: What can farmers plant to reduce wind erosion?
items.e: Windbreaks slow the wind.

items.q: Plant roots grow into cracks in rocks. What kind of weathering is this?
items.e: Roots can split rocks.

items.q: Which change happens very quickly?
c: a glacier wearing down a mountain
items.e: Some changes take seconds, others take millions of years.

items.q: Emma finds a scientist's report that a rockslide closed a trail in a few seconds. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It took seconds.

items.q: A farmer leaves bare soil all winter. What can happen in spring?
c: Melting snow and rain wash the soil away.
items.e: Cover crops protect soil.

items.q: A river bank is wearing away near a farm. Which solution would help most?
c: remove the plants on the bank
plant shrubs and trees along the bank
items.e: Roots hold soil.

items.q: Strong wind picks up loose sand from a dune. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: What is erosion?
c: the moving of soil and rock pieces by water, wind or ice
the breaking of rock in place only
items.e: Erosion carries sediment away.

items.q: Sand is pushed along a beach by waves arriving at an angle. Which process is this?
items.e: Transportation carries the pieces to a new place.

items.q: Heavy rain washes soil off a bare hillside. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: Leah finds a video of mud sliding over a road in 1 minute. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It happened in 1 minute.

items.q: Which word means dropping sand, mud or pebbles in a new place?
items.e: Deposition happens when the moving water or wind slows down.

items.q: Waves drop sand in a sheltered bay, making a wide beach. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: Which helps stop soil erosion on a hillside?
items.e: Roots hold soil in place.

items.q: A desert rock is shaped like a mushroom by sand blowing near the ground. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: Fine sand is blown off a ploughed field on a windy day. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: A storm surge washes away the front of a sand dune at the beach. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is waves.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the sand dunes of K'gari (Fraser Island)?
items.e: Wind and waves dropped huge amounts of sand.

items.q: Waves carve a cave into the bottom of a limestone cliff. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is waves.

items.q: Why do farmers plant rows of trees between fields?
c: to slow the wind and reduce soil erosion
items.e: Windbreaks protect soil.

items.q: Loose soil slides down a hillside cut for a new road. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is gravity.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes third?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: Where does a river drop most of its sediment?
c: where it slows down, like at its mouth
at the top of a waterfall
items.e: Slow water cannot carry as much.

items.q: Boulders tumble down a gorge wall and pile up at the bottom. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is gravity.

items.q: What is a glacier?
c: a huge, slow-moving body of ice
items.e: Glaciers erode the land as they move.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the Three Sisters in the Blue Mountains?
c: weathering and erosion by wind and rain
items.e: Wind and rain wore away the softer sandstone around them.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the wide floodplain beside the Hawkesbury River?
c: weathering and erosion by wind and rain
items.e: Floods dropped layers of mud on the land.

items.q: Rocks fall down a steep slope after heavy rain loosens them. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is gravity.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the mouth of the Murray River?
items.e: The river slows and drops sand and mud where it meets the sea.

items.q: Pebbles on a beach are rolled smooth by the sea. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is waves.

items.q: What is weathering?
c: the breaking down of rock into smaller pieces
dropping sediment in a new place
items.e: Weathering breaks; erosion moves.

items.q: Which change to the land takes the longest?
c: a river carving a deep valley
items.e: River valleys form over thousands of years.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes second?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: Chloe looks at this picture. This storm floods a town. Is it a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It takes hours or days.

items.q: Chloe compares a volcano erupting and a river carving a canyon. Which happens faster?
items.e: A volcano erupting takes hours or days; a river carving a canyon takes millions of years.

items.q: Noah looks at this picture. This volcano erupts. Is it a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It takes hours or days.

items.q: Sofia looks at this picture. This storm floods a town. How long does it take?
items.e: It is a fast change.

items.q: Maya reads: “A glacier slides down a valley and shapes it.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes thousands of years, so it is slow.

items.q: Why do rocks in a fast river become smooth and round?
c: They bump and rub against each other as the water carries them.
items.e: Moving water erodes rock.

items.q: Owen compares a volcano erupting and mud turning into rock. Which happens faster?
items.e: A volcano erupting takes hours or days; mud turning into rock takes millions of years.

items.q: Olivia compares a flood and waves wearing away a cliff. Which happens slower?
items.e: Waves wearing away a cliff takes hundreds of years; a flood takes hours or days.

items.q: Ethan compares a rock wearing into sand and a storm wave hitting a dune. Which happens slower?
c: a storm wave hitting a dune
items.e: A rock wearing into sand takes thousands of years; a storm wave hitting a dune takes hours.

items.q: Emma reads: “A tall mountain wears down and gets shorter.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes millions of years, so it is slow.

items.q: Maya looks at this picture. This volcano erupts. How long does it take?
items.e: It is a fast change.

items.q: Ava looks at this picture. A river carved this canyon. How long does it take?
items.e: It is a slow change.

items.q: Jayden reads: “A big storm wave knocks down part of a sand dune.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a fast change: hours.

items.q: Ava compares an earthquake and a cave forming. Which happens slower?
items.e: A cave forming takes thousands of years; an earthquake takes seconds or minutes.

items.q: Zoe reads: “Layers of mud pile up and turn into rock.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes millions of years, so it is slow.

items.q: Arjun compares a storm wave hitting a dune and a river carving a canyon. Which happens faster?
c: a storm wave hitting a dune
items.e: A storm wave hitting a dune takes hours; a river carving a canyon takes millions of years.

items.q: Leah reads: “A volcano erupts and lava covers a hill.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes hours or days, so it is fast.

items.q: Sofia reads: “A glacier slides down a valley and shapes it.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a slow change: thousands of years.

items.q: Sofia reads: “A flood fills a town's streets with water.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes hours or days, so it is fast.

items.q: Aiden looks at this picture. Wind and rain wear down this mountain. How long does it take?
items.e: It is a slow change.

items.q: Can a slow change still change the land a lot?
c: Yes, over a very long time.
items.e: Slow does not mean small.

items.q: What does 'weathering' mean?
c: rock slowly breaking into smaller pieces
items.e: Wind, water and ice break rock.

items.q: Which change is fast?
items.e: Earthquakes last seconds or minutes.

items.q: Emma finds photos of a cliff taken 50 years apart that look almost the same. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: The cliff barely changed in 50 years.

items.q: How long can a big canyon take to form?
items.e: Rivers cut rock very slowly.

items.q: Which variable should stay the same when testing how slope affects erosion?
c: the amount of soil washed away
items.e: Only the slope should change.

items.q: Sofia finds a video of lava pouring down a volcano in one night. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It happened in one night.

items.q: Where can you find out about Earth changes?
items.e: Use more than one source.

items.q: Why are retaining walls built on steep slopes?
c: to hold soil and rock in place
items.e: Walls reduce landslides.

items.q: A beach lost 3 m of sand in a big storm. Over the next 6 months it gained 1 m back each 2 months. How wide is it now compared with before the storm?
items.e: Erosion in the storm, deposition afterwards: 1 m × 3 = 3 m.

items.q: Ella builds two model sand dunes. She covers one with spinifex grass cuttings and blows a fan at both. What is she testing?
items.e: The plants are the variable she changed.

items.q: Mateo says, 'Weathering and erosion are the same thing.' Which reply is best?
c: Erosion breaks rock; weathering moves it.
Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves the pieces away.
items.e: One breaks, the other moves.

items.q: Zoe photographs a creek bank every month for a year. The bank moves back 40 cm. Which question does this answer?
c: How fast is the creek eroding its bank?
How many fish live in the creek?
What will the weather be tomorrow?
items.e: Repeated photos measure slow change.

items.q: Noah finds a book that says the canyon took millions of years to form. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: Millions of years is very slow.

items.q: Which agent of erosion shaped the sand dunes at Sandbanks Provincial Park?
items.e: Wind moves sand into dunes.

items.q: Kai blows through a straw at a pile of sand and gravel. What does he see?
c: The fine sand moves further than the gravel.
The gravel moves further than the sand.
items.e: Wind can carry light pieces further.

items.q: In a stream table, which change would carry the most sand away?
c: the same slope and no water
a flatter slope and less water
a steeper slope and more water
items.e: Faster water erodes and carries more.

items.q: Which change is slow?
items.e: Canyons take millions of years.

items.q: Ethan finds a news story about an earthquake that lasted 30 seconds. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It lasted only seconds.

items.q: Chloe pours 500 mL of water on two trays of soil. One is bare; one has grass. The bare tray loses 120 g of soil. Which result is most likely for the grass tray?
items.e: Grass roots hold the soil.

items.q: Liam says the Grand Canyon formed in one big flood. Is he right?
c: No. A river carved it over millions of years.
items.e: Canyons form slowly.

items.q: Noah learns: “A river cuts its canyon about 3 mm deeper per year.” At this rate, about how much deeper will it get in 10000 years?
Hana learns: “The Himalayas rise about 10 mm per year.” At this rate, about how much taller will they get in 100000 years?
Sand blasts against a rock in a dust storm and smooths it. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: Ava learns: “A river cuts its canyon about 3 mm deeper per year.” At this rate, about how much deeper will it get in 100000 years?
Kai wants evidence that a beach is wearing away. Which source helps most?
c: photos of the beach taken every year for 20 years
items.e: Photos over time show slow change.

items.q: Emma learns: “The Atlantic Ocean widens about 3 cm per year.” At this rate, about how much wider will it get in 1000000 years?
Noah reads that waves wear back a sea cliff. Does this change happen quickly (minutes to days) or slowly (thousands to millions of years)?
items.e: Many large landforms are built by slow processes over very long times.

items.q: A tree root grows into a crack and slowly pushes the rock apart. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: What is deposition?
c: dropping eroded sediment in a new place
items.e: Rivers drop sand where they slow down.

items.q: Maya reads that a meteor makes a crater. Does this change happen quickly (minutes to days) or slowly (thousands to millions of years)?
c: It happens only on other planets.
items.e: Earthquakes, landslides and eruptions change the surface quickly in small areas.

items.q: Ethan learns: “A river cuts its canyon about 1 mm deeper per year.” At this rate, about how much deeper will it get in 10000 years?
Where does a river drop most of its sand and mud?
c: where it slows down, such as at its mouth
at the top of a waterfall
at the fastest part of the river
items.e: Slow water cannot carry as much.

items.q: Chloe learns: “A river cuts its canyon about 2 mm deeper per year.” At this rate, about how much deeper will it get in 10000 years?
Layers of sand settle at the bottom of a lake over many years. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: Ethan reads that wind shapes desert rocks into arches. Does this change happen quickly (minutes to days) or slowly (thousands to millions of years)?
items.e: Many large landforms are built by slow processes over very long times.

items.q: Lucas reads that a rockfall drops boulders from a cliff. Does this change happen quickly (minutes to days) or slowly (thousands to millions of years)?
c: It happens only on other planets.
items.e: Earthquakes, landslides and eruptions change the surface quickly in small areas.

items.q: Rain running off a parking lot cuts a channel in the dirt beside it. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is running water.

items.q: Chloe reads that a landslide covered a road in 2 minutes. Which word fits?
items.e: 2 minutes is fast.

items.q: Emma reads that continents drift apart and an ocean widens. Does this change happen quickly (minutes to days) or slowly (thousands to millions of years)?
items.e: Many large landforms are built by slow processes over very long times.
